newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Experts see tighter Fed on the horizon.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Experts see tighter Fed on the horizon.

text.p: The Federal Reserve will probably have to tap the brakes again in May or July if it really wants to slow down a robust U.S. economy, said a majority of economists polled by Reuters on Wednesday.
Fifteen of 31 economists said they expect the Fed to lift the federal funds rate an additional 25 basis points at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on May 20.
But 23 of 28 pundits predicted that by early July, the Fed will have raised that target rate to at least 5.75 percent.

The experts' prediction of another rate-hike followed the Fed's widely anticipated decision on Tuesday to ratchet up the key fed funds rate a quarter-point to 5.50 percent. The central bank left the discount rate unchanged at 5.0 percent.
Tuesday's rate hike is likely to be the first of at least two upward moves, with the prospect of a third before yearend, said Tim O'Neill, chief economist at Harris Bank/Bank of Montreal.
"(The Fed) will not have to go beyond 6.0 percent on the federal funds rate (because) there is not that much momentum in the economy," he said.

O'Neill asserted that the economy already has some built-in dampening effects, such as the strong dollar's influence on trade. But the Fed will certainly keep a wary eye open for continued signs of economic strengthening, he said. "The Fed is trying to protect the Goldilocks economy from the good economic news bears," O'Neill added.
Analysts said for the Fed to tighten again, it would need to see signs that the economy was continuing to grow above its commonly perceived non-inflationary potential rate of about 2.0-2.5 percent.

Currently, there are signs of pressure in the labor market and a potential for strong consumer demand boosting inflation, they said. Therefore, most Wall Street experts cheered the Fed's move Tuesday and said it bolstered Fed Chairman Alan Greesnpan's credibility.
"A lot of the decision in May will depend on the (data) that come out in the next few weeks," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and an economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
If the data continue to signal strong economic growth, Flanagan said, there is a "better-than-even" chance that the central bank will move rates again in May.
But he said the Fed will probably not engage in a tightening cycle that will push the federal funds rate as high as 7.0 percent.
Don Maude, chief U.S. economist at Scotia Capital Markets Inc, concurred, calling any subsequent moves a "mini-cycle" of tightening.
"I would compare this as the flipside of the easing cycle (the Fed) was on in 1995," Maude said, referring to the central bank's gradual reduction in fed funds to 5.25 percent from 6.0 percent.
The Fed eased rates -- in 25-basis-point increments -- in July and December of 1995, and on January 31 1996.
Now, the Fed will probably take the funds rate back to 6.0 percent from 5.25 percent, but in a shorter period, Maude said.
